      If every — time control had its own rating, a — player rated — would be rated about:
      
      Higher means that queue is easier: at the same rating, the players you meet there are weaker. These figures are for someone who plays both about equally. If you mostly play one time control you will do better in it than this suggests, and worse in the others.
    

    
      
        The gap depends on your rating
        How many points higher (above the line) or lower (below it) a — player would be rated in each other time control, at each — rating, in —. Shaded bands are 95% intervals; a line stops where its interval would be wider than ±16 points. Click to pick a rating.
        
      

      
        Month by month
        The same gaps each month, for — players rated —. Click to pick a month.
        
      

      
        How this is measured
        
          All time controls in a category share one rating, so there is no second rating to compare. Instead the report takes players who played both time controls in the same month.
          In each time control, it compares how they actually scored with what their own and their opponents' ratings predicted, and turns the difference into rating points.
          People do better in whichever time control they play most. To cancel that out, it averages the players who mostly play one with those who mostly play the other. What is left is how much tougher one queue is than the other at the same rating.
          Each figure is smoothed across nearby ratings and months the same way as the conversions between categories: a weighted local fit that widens only where few players play both.
        
      
    
  

  
  
    
      The data
      Every rated lobby game (the "Rated Bullet game", "Rated Blitz game" and similar events) in the Lichess standard-chess open database from — to —: — games once bot games are removed. Tournament games are not in this copy of the data, which suits the queue-size measure. The 2026 figures cover January to September only.
      Lichess places a game in a category by its estimated duration, base time plus 40 times the increment: under 30 seconds is UltraBullet (here only ¼+0), under 3 minutes Bullet, under 8 Blitz, under 25 Rapid, and the rest Classical. Each category has one Glicko-2 rating shared by all its time controls. Rapid did not exist before November 2017, when Classical covered everything from 8 minutes up, so the old Classical pool is shown on its own as "Classical (pre-Nov 2017)". New Rapid ratings were seeded from Classical at the split.

      Between categories
      
        Only contemporaneous play counts. A pair of ratings is recorded at a moment when both were current: the player had just played in one category and had played in the other within the last 30 days.
        No provisional ratings. Rating deviation is not in the data, so it is worked out from each game's rating change. Both ratings must be established (deviation 75 or less, where Lichess shows a rating as rankable) and the player must have at least 20 games in each category.
        Frequent dual players count most. Each player-month gets a weight equal to the smaller of their game counts in the two categories that month, capped at 30, so someone who plays both every day counts far more than someone who dabbles, without letting a handful of accounts dominate.
        Drift is handled month by month. Every figure belongs to one month and borrows only from the months around it, so a conversion always describes the pools as they were at that time.
        Two kinds of answer. The average is the expected rating in the other category for people at your rating. Because nobody's two ratings move in lockstep, it regresses toward the middle, so A to B and B to A are not inverses. The same-percentile rating matches ranks among the dual players instead, and is symmetric.
        Smoothing. Each figure is a weighted fit through the player-months nearby in both rating and time: a local-linear smoother (the core of loess) with weights falling off smoothly with distance in rating points and in months, and a linear trend in time so the latest months are not dragged toward the past. The window is ±25 rating points and ±2.5 months where data is dense, and widens step by step to at most ±150 points and ±13 months until about 1,500 player-months are inside it, so busy pairs keep near-monthly detail and rare ones borrow from their neighbours. The spread of players comes from the same window after moving each neighbour along the fitted slope. The same-percentile rating and the method comparison are yearly.
        Always rising. A higher rating in one category should never mean a lower expected rating in the other, but where few players hold both, noise can make a smoothed curve dip. Each month's curve is therefore made non-decreasing (a weighted isotonic regression): a stretch that dips becomes a flat run at its precision-weighted average, and rising stretches are left alone. The spread of players is treated the same way. This moved about 3% of the figures, mostly rough ones, and almost always by less than their 95% interval.
        Intervals. 95% intervals come from a jackknife over 16 groups of players. The middle half and middle 80% describe how individual players spread around the average.
      

      Within a category
      
        Time controls in one category move the same rating, so there are no two ratings to compare. Instead, for each player who played two of them in the same month (at least 5 games in each), the report measures how much better or worse they scored in each than both players' ratings predicted, and takes the difference.
        Player-months are combined with random-effects weights, so players with many games count more but saturate. A player's rating here is their average rating in those games.
        Each month is labelled by which time control had at least two thirds of the player's games in that pair. Players do better in the one they play most, so the figure shown is the midpoint between those who mostly play one and those who mostly play the other: the gap for someone with no preference. Players who split their games evenly land close to that midpoint, which supports it.
        Each group's average is a weighted local fit in rating and month, like the conversions between categories: ±25 rating points and ±2.5 months where data is dense, widening (to at most ±150 points and ±13 months) until each group has about 400 player-months. A figure is shown only where its 95% interval is narrower than ±16 points.
        The time controls compared are the current home-page quick pairings plus each category's three most played over the whole data, which adds only ½+0 Bullet and 15+15 Classical.
      

      Limits
      
        Dual players are not a random sample of everyone. A 1500 Rapid player who also plays Blitz may differ from one who never does.
        Lichess changed how fast rating deviation grows between games in August to September 2019 and again in January 2020, which shifts how quickly ratings settle around those dates.
        Near the ends of each curve, and for the rarer categories, few players hold both ratings. The report marks a conversion as rough when its 95% interval is wider than ±50 points and leaves it out when wider than ±100. Read a rough figure as a range.

title: David Nield
text:
I am currently a Staff Data Scientist at Walmart Connect, where I was the first data scientist hired on the Advertising Sales team. My work focuses on bridging the gap between complex data infrastructure and executive decision-making. I build and maintain models for sales revenue forecasting, sales quota/incentive planning, advertiser churn prediction, and the complex data pipelines that power the dashboards used by hundreds of unique daily active business users.
Prior to working at Walmart Connect, I worked for four years at Callisto Media Inc., a data-driven book publishing start-up, where I maintained the topic demand model at the core of the business up until its sale to Penguin Random House in May 2023. Before Callisto, I was a PhD Student in Political Science at the University of California, Berkeley, where I conducted research on political misinformation, religious prejudice, political contributor networks, and “small world” network structures.
I have spent the majority of my career working on small teams of data scientists, which has made me a data science generalist. I have practical experience working directly with business executives and leading projects with both business stakeholders and technical contributors from multiple teams, as well as technical experience in time series forecasting, supervised machine learning, A/B testing, observational causal inference, and database design and architecture.
In my free time, I enjoy playing chess, watching Ohio State football, camping and hiking with my wife, Samantha, and my one-year-old (as of February 2026) daughter, Violet, around where we live in Southern California.

title: What happened to the Rossolimo?
text:
What happened to the Rossolimo?
In November 2018, the Lichess Openings Explorer shows that the Rossolimo had a sudden surge in popularity, growing from occurring in 0.291% of games in October to 0.383% of games in November, a small (0.092%) increase in nominal terms, but a huge jump (31%!) in relative terms. Given the suddenness of the spike after over a year of stability, then a gradual decline back to its normal 0.3% levels over the next few years, it’s extremely unlikely that this was just random noise.



The Rossolimo’s popularity on the Lichess Opening Explorer, with a sharp spike in November 2018.


Followers of competitive chess might notice right away that this was the month that the 2018 World Chess Championship started, featuring Fabiano Caruana as the challenger to Magnus Carlsen, and the obvious reason for this sudden spike in the Rossolimo’s popularity was due to the fact that the Rossolimo featured prominently in this title match, with Caruana choosing 1. e4 for all of the non-tie break games in the match, and Magnus choosing the Sicilian, intending to play the Sveshnikov in the Open Sicilian, during all of these games. Rather than going into the Open Sicilian, Caruana opted for the Rossolimo in each of his first three games with White, but after failing to break through and drawing all three, he switched to the Open Sicilian to try to break through Magnus’s Sveshnikov in his next three games, which also ended in draws, sending the match into tiebreak games. The rest, as we say, is history.
It seems likely the competitive chess watchers following the match decided to pick up and try using the openings being used in the most watched match of the year, being played between the world #1 and #2 at the time, both rated over 2800 and only 3 rating points separating them at the time of the match.
But here’s an interesting question: was this increase in popularity driven by White players switching to the Rossolimo? or by Black players switching to the Nc6 Sicilian? Or both?
You could answer this by just checking and recording the popularity of each of the prior positions in the path to the Rossolimo, and seeing whether we see this same graph shape in each of them. We do, but the relative change gets bigger the deeper into the opening you go:

The changes in 1. e4’s and 1… c5’s popularity are indiscernible from random noise in the graph, but the changes compound with each additional move.
But yes, just from the changes in the popularity of 2… Nc6 and 3. Bb5 you can reasonably infer that the aggregate popularity of the Rossolimo was probably driven by some combination of White players giving 3. Bb5 a try, and Black players giving Nc6 Sicilian a try. But then, how do you quantify the relative impact? And which color is the subsequent falloff in popularity attributable to? Checking the graphs of all of these positions in order to answer these kinds of questions is kind of a pain in the butt…
Which leads me to my point: the issue with “opening explorers” is that they don’t really give you statistics about the opening, they give you statistics about a position. For example, the graph above shows what percentage of games reach a position, and the table below shows how many games reached it over the selected time span, how often the player to move (White, in this case) plays each legal move from it, and the score rate for the position and for each move.



The Lichess Opening Explorer table for the Rossolimo position




What an opening explorer should be able to tell you
1. How often you would get to play the opening, if it was in your repertoire,
2. How opponents would see the opening when facing players other than you,
3. Is the increase or decline in the popularity of an opening being driven by one color not playing as often? or because the other color isn’t giving them the chance to play it as often?
These are all the types of questions that chess opening data nerds like me would want to know, and they’re super simple to calculate/answer given the data within these tables, but it requires you to record the sequence of probabilities, not just the probabilities you see in the current position.
Let’s take question 1: if we wanted to calculate how often we would get to play the Rossolimo as White, all we need to do is take the probability that Black plays 1… c5 when faced with 1. e4 (which is 17.3% across all Lichess rated standard games, excluding arena and swiss tournaments and bots) and multiply that by the probability that Black plays 2… Nc6 after we play 2. Nf3 (which is 42.5%). 17.3% x 42.5% = 7.4% probability that White gets to play the Rossolimo in any given game. That’s way higher than the 0.383% probability we saw earlier, right? That’s because we take our moves as given, we don’t need to include the probability that we will play 1. e4, 2. Nf3, or 3. Bb5 in the calculation because we know we will play them.
Answering question 2 means doing the exact opposite: given that our opponent plays the Nc6 Sicilian, the probability that they would face the Rossolimo means multiplying the probability that their opponent will play 1. e4 (59%), will respond to their 1… c5 move with 2. Nf3 (52.3%), and then respond to their 2… Nc6 move with 3. Bb5 (12.7%), for a final probability of 3.9%.
One fun corollary of the answers to questions 1 and 2 is that, with these probabilities, you can then calculate how much more experience in the opening than you will have than your opponent by simply taking the ratio of the percentage of the time you get to play it over the probability of the time they will face it, so White Rossolimo players will have 7.4% / 3.9% = 1.9x as much experience in Rossolimo positions as their opponents will.



The Rossolimo’s move path: each move’s share among the games that reached the position before it, with W (White’s moves) and B (Black’s moves) multiplying to the Rossolimo’s overall popularity.


Finally, these two probabilities also helps us answer our third question, because we can now attribute the change in the popularity of the position to each color, because the popularity of a position is simply the product of these two probabilities, and by decomposing it into these two numbers, we can precisely calculate how much of the percentage change is due to changes in what White plays when given the chance versus changes in what Black plays when given the chance.
Any math nerds might notice that all of these calculations are all just products, i.e. the probability of the Rossolimo is P(1.e4) x P(1… c5) x P(2.Nf3) x P(2… Nc6) x P(3. Bb5), and the cool thing about products – okay, maybe only cool if you’re a math nerd – is that you can take their log, so that these probabilities become additive, meaning that when we take that Lichess opening popularity graph and put it on the log scale, we can also graph the net contribution of White and Black to that popularity. This sets up something like a nice “waterfall” plot, where, when both White and Black play the prerequisite moves for an opening more or they both play it less, then the position popularity’s net change line on a log scale will rest on top of (or at the bottom of) the relative changes in these question #1 and question #2 probabilities, and if they pull in opposite directions, the position’s net change in popularity line will be based on just the difference between the two contributions.


So, which color really drove the Rossolimo’s surge, and subsequent decline, in popularity?
If we just choose a starting point to index the change to, we can create a plot like the one below, which shows the change in the popularity of the Rossolimo in relative terms to its popularity in January 2017 and provides a clean answer to our question, and quantifies what we had to look at multiple Lichess opening explorer graphs to see earlier: the Rossolimo indeed got about 30% more popular on November 2018, and it was, initially, due to both White and Black playing it when they had the chance. However, the increased popularity among White players was relatively short-lived, with White playing the Rossolimo no more frequently (in terms of % of games that they play it when given the opportunity) than in January 2017 by just two months later. Almost all of the residual increase in popularity of the Rossolimo is attributable to Black players playing 1… c5 and 2… Nc6 more frequently during 2019-2020 than they had in 2017-2018, so White players who kept in their repertoire just had more opportunities to use it. This is, perhaps, itself attributable that Magnus Carlsen ended up winning the match, as Caruana was unsuccessful in breaking through Magnus’s Sicilian with his Rossolimo, to the point that Caruana ended up switching to the Open Sicilian later in the match.



Who moved it: the change in the Rossolimo’s popularity since January 2017 on a log scale. Blue bars are White’s contribution, orange bars are Black’s, and the black line is the net change; the parts add exactly.




Wrapping up
I want to make one thing super clear: this post is not meant to be a criticism of Lichess, the design of its opening explorer, or anything of the sort. The visual simplicity of Lichess’s database table is one of its greatest strengths, and adding any of these visualizations/statistics would require adding a substantial amount of visual clutter and significantly complicating their design, for capabilities only a niche set of opening data nerds like me would ever use.
This post, and all of the tools that I’ve built on the Openings section of my website (which are interactive and available for free so you can explore these and other stats for any named opening, across any time control, rating bracket, or time period) wouldn’t be possible without Lichess making their data freely available to the public. I am eternally grateful for their contributions to the chess data world, with special thanks to Christopher Akiki for his work making Lichess’s data even more accessible on Huggingface.
This was just a hobby project of mine to 1. make it easier to answer the types of questions that I like to investigate, 2. see how easy it is to host an interactive dashboard on my personal website, and 3. give me the chance to write about something that I think is cool.
I hope you think it’s cool too. Give the Openings section of my website a whirl. I’ve added little one-click export “Download” buttons for exporting any visualizations you make as pngs for making it easy to share what you find.
